where $\vec{v} \cdot \vec{\sigma} \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{3} v_{i} \sigma_{i}$.
This exercise is generalized in Problem 2.1 on page 117.
Another important matrix function is the trace of a matrix.
The trace of $A$ is defined to be the sum of its diagonal elements,

$$
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{tr}(A) \equiv \sum_{i} A_{i i} \tag{2.59}
\end{equation*}
$$

The trace is easily seen to be cyclic, $\operatorname{tr}(A B)=\operatorname{tr}(B A)$, and linear, $\operatorname{tr}(A+B)= \operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B), \operatorname{tr}(z A)=z \operatorname{tr}(A)$, where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary matrices, and $z$ is a complex number.
Furthermore, from the cyclic property it follows that the trace of a matrix is invariant under the unitary similarity transformation $A \rightarrow U A U^{\dagger}$, as $\operatorname{tr}\left(U A U^{\dagger}\right)= \operatorname{tr}\left(U^{\dagger} U A\right)=\operatorname{tr}(A)$.
In light of this result, it makes sense to define the trace of an operator $A$ to be the trace of any matrix representation of $A$.
